```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(data.table)
library(readxl)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)

options(width = 110)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "code")

# --- toy customer data for the opening example ---
# three overlapping groups: occasional, frequent small-basket, big spenders
set.seed(42)
toy_spec <- list(c(6, 2.5, 300, 130), c(15, 3, 1050, 250), c(14, 3, 500, 140))
toy <- rbindlist(lapply(seq_along(toy_spec), function(i) data.table(
  purchases = pmax(0, round(rnorm(20, toy_spec[[i]][1], toy_spec[[i]][2]))),
  spend     = pmax(20, rnorm(20, toy_spec[[i]][3], toy_spec[[i]][4])),
  truth     = LETTERS[i])))
km_toy <- kmeans(scale(toy[, .(purchases, spend)]), centers = 3, nstart = 20)
toy[, cluster := as.factor(km_toy$cluster)]
# cluster averages, ordered by spend: occasional, frequent small-basket, big spenders
toy_c <- toy[, .(purchases = mean(purchases), spend = mean(spend)), by = cluster][order(spend)]
fmt_toy <- function(i) sprintf("about %.0f purchases, $%s", toy_c$purchases[i],
                               format(round(toy_c$spend[i], -1), big.mark = ","))

# --- office-store segmentation data ---
dd <- as.data.table(read_excel("code/data/segmentation_office.xlsx",
                               sheet = "SegmentationData"))
ratings <- dd[, .(variety_of_choice, electronics, furniture,
                  quality_of_service, low_prices, return_policy)]

set.seed(123)
wss <- sapply(2:10, function(k) kmeans(ratings, centers = k, nstart = 20)$tot.withinss)
elbow <- data.table(k = 2:10, wss = wss)

set.seed(123)
km <- kmeans(ratings, centers = 3, nstart = 20)
dd[, cluster := as.factor(km$cluster)]

pca <- prcomp(ratings, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
scores <- data.table(pca$x[, 1:2], cluster = dd$cluster)
loadings <- as.data.table(pca$rotation[, 1:2], keep.rownames = "attribute")
plain_names <- c(variety_of_choice = "variety", electronics = "electronics",
                 furniture = "furniture", quality_of_service = "quality of service",
                 low_prices = "low prices", return_policy = "return policy")
loadings[, attribute := plain_names[attribute]]

seg_cols <- c("1" = "#990000", "2" = "#0072B2", "3" = "#E69F00")
seg_labs <- c("1: bargain hunters", "2: one-stop shoppers", "3: service seekers")

# --- brand perceptual-map data ---
brands <- fread("code/data/perceptual_map_office.csv")
pca_b  <- prcomp(brands[, 2:7], center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
scores_b   <- data.table(pca_b$x[, 1:2], brand = brands$brand)
loadings_b <- as.data.table(pca_b$rotation[, 1:2], keep.rownames = "attribute")
loadings_b[, attribute := sub(" score$", "", gsub("_", " ", attribute))]
```

## A different kind of question {.smaller-90}

Every model so far had an **outcome** to predict: a listing's price, then
whether it is a gem. Today there is no outcome. There are just customers, described by
numbers, and one question: **who is similar to whom?**

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What changes**

- No $Y$, no coefficients, no stars: the algorithm proposes **groups**
- This is called **unsupervised** learning: nothing tells the algorithm
  what the right answer is
:::
::: {.column style="width: 44%; margin-left: 5%;"}
**What stays**

- The data is still rows and columns, and **you** choose the columns
- The output still means nothing until **you** interpret it
- Still **not causation**: clusters describe, they do not explain
:::
:::::

## Why marketers cluster (and map) {.smaller-90}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
Grouping similar customers is **segmentation**, and almost everything in
marketing is segment-specific:

- **Messaging**: bargain hunters get the discount email, service seekers
  get the concierge pitch
- **Product and pricing**: which features matter to which group, and who
  will pay for them
- **Budget**: which segments are growing, and where the next dollar goes
- **Positioning**: the same kind of data, mapped, shows who competes with
  whom and where the gaps are: the **perceptual map** on the right
:::
::: {.column style="width: 47%; margin-left: 5%;"}
```{r perceptual-sketch}
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 4.4
cars <- data.table(
  brand = c("Toyota", "Honda", "Kia", "Volvo", "Mercedes", "BMW", "Porsche", "Mazda"),
  x = c(-2.2, -1.7, -2.4, 1.3, 2.2, 2.1, 2.8, -0.9),
  y = c(-1.2, -0.5, 0.2, -2.0, -0.4, 1.0, 2.2, 1.3)
)
ggplot(cars, aes(x, y, label = brand)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(color = "#990000", size = 3.5) +
  geom_text_repel(size = 4.6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-3.4, 3.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2.9, 2.9)) +
  labs(title = "The car market, as customers see it",
       x = "← affordable    ·    premium →",
       y = "← practical    ·    sporty →") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
```

:::
:::::

::: {.box}
Two tools today. **K-means** finds the groups. **PCA** draws the map you
need to *see* them, and it powers the perceptual map.
:::

# Finding Groups: K-Means {.divider}

## Sixty customers, two numbers

```{r toy-plain}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.4
p_toy <- ggplot(toy, aes(x = purchases, y = spend)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8, color = "grey35") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(title = "Customers: Purchases vs. Total Spend, Last Year",
       x = "Purchases last year", y = "Total spend last year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p_toy
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Each dot is a customer: how often they bought, and how much they spent in
total. How many groups do you see, and how would you describe each one?
:::

## The same chart, after k-means {.smaller-90 .nostretch}

```{r toy-clustered}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.9
cents <- toy[, .(purchases = mean(purchases), spend = mean(spend)), by = cluster]
p_toy +
  geom_point(data = toy, aes(color = cluster), size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_point(data = cents, shape = 4, size = 6, stroke = 2, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = unname(seg_cols), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "The Same Customers, Colored by K-Means (k = 3)")
```

- The only thing we told k-means is the **number of clusters, k = 3**. It
  found the groups from the data alone. Where your eyes hesitated, it drew
  the borders by **distance**, the same way every time
- The **X** marks each cluster's center. Read the centers and the groups get
  names: **occasional shoppers** (`r fmt_toy(1)`), **frequent small-basket
  shoppers** (`r fmt_toy(2)`), and **big spenders** (`r fmt_toy(3)`)
- Eyes can handle 2 columns and 60 customers, not **6 columns and thousands
  of customers**. The algorithm can, with the same logic

## How k-means works {.smaller-90}

You pick **k**, the number of clusters. The algorithm does the rest:

1. Place k **centers** at random
2. **Assign** every customer to the nearest center
3. **Move** each center to the middle of the customers assigned to it
4. Repeat 2 and 3 until the centers stop moving

- On the last chart, that is: drop three **X**'s at random, color every
  dot by its nearest X, move each X to the middle of its color, repeat.
  The X's you saw are where they stopped
- "Nearest" means plain **distance** between rows of numbers, so every
  column you feed it counts
- The random start means results can vary from run to run. In practice,
  k-means is run many times (say, 20) from different starts, and the best
  result is kept

::: {.box}
K-means never sees names, labels, or meanings. It groups rows of numbers by
distance. Everything the clusters *mean* comes later, from you.
:::

## K-means, step by step {.nostretch}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 56%;"}
```{r kmeans-steps}
#| output: asis
# Run k-means one step at a time on the 60 toy customers (the same algorithm
# kmeans() uses, from one random start), and save one picture per step
X_toy <- scale(toy[, .(purchases, spend)])
mu_toy <- attr(X_toy, "scaled:center"); sd_toy <- attr(X_toy, "scaled:scale")
to_orig <- function(C) data.table(purchases = C[, 1] * sd_toy[1] + mu_toy[1],
                                  spend     = C[, 2] * sd_toy[2] + mu_toy[2])
set.seed(2048)
C <- X_toy[sample(nrow(X_toy), 3), , drop = FALSE]
steps <- list(); prev <- rep(0L, nrow(X_toy))
repeat {
  dist2 <- sapply(1:3, function(k)
    rowSums((X_toy - matrix(C[k, ], nrow(X_toy), 2, byrow = TRUE))^2))
  a <- max.col(-dist2)
  steps[[length(steps) + 1]] <- list(C = C, a = a, switched = sum(a != prev & prev > 0))
  if (all(a == prev)) break
  prev <- a
  C <- t(sapply(1:3, function(k) colMeans(X_toy[a == k, , drop = FALSE])))
}
# match colors to the clusters on the earlier chart
final_a <- steps[[length(steps)]]$a
lab <- sapply(1:3, function(k) names(which.max(table(toy$cluster[final_a == k]))))

xlim_toy <- c(0, max(toy$purchases) + 1)
ylim_toy <- c(0, max(toy$spend) * 1.05)
draw <- function(title, subtitle = NULL, a = NULL, C = NULL, C_old = NULL, links = FALSE) {
  d <- toy[, .(purchases, spend)]
  d[, col := if (is.null(a)) "grey" else lab[a]]
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(purchases, spend))
  if (links) {
    cc <- to_orig(C)
    d[, `:=`(cx = cc$purchases[a], cy = cc$spend[a])]
    p <- p + geom_segment(data = d, aes(xend = cx, yend = cy, color = col),
                          alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.4)
  }
  p <- p + geom_point(aes(color = col), size = 3, alpha = 0.85)
  if (!is.null(C_old)) {
    co <- to_orig(C_old); cn <- to_orig(C)
    arr <- data.table(x = co$purchases, y = co$spend, xend = cn$purchases, yend = cn$spend)
    p <- p +
      geom_point(data = co, shape = 4, size = 6, stroke = 2, color = "grey60") +
      geom_segment(data = arr, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")), linewidth = 0.9)
  }
  if (!is.null(C)) {
    cc <- to_orig(C); cc[, col := lab]
    p <- p +
      geom_point(data = cc, shape = 4, size = 8, stroke = 4.5, color = "black") +
      geom_point(data = cc, aes(color = col), shape = 4, size = 7, stroke = 2.6)
  }
  p + scale_color_manual(values = c(seg_cols, grey = "grey35"), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = xlim_toy) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar, limits = ylim_toy) +
    # equal scales: one standard deviation looks the same length on both axes,
    # so the X that looks nearest is the X that IS nearest
    coord_fixed(ratio = sd_toy[1] / sd_toy[2]) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle,
         x = "Purchases last year", y = "Total spend last year") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}

frames <- list(
  draw("Step 1: drop 3 centers", "anywhere, at random", C = steps[[1]]$C),
  draw("Step 2: assign", "each customer takes the color of its nearest X",
       a = steps[[1]]$a, C = steps[[1]]$C, links = TRUE))
for (i in 2:length(steps)) {
  frames[[length(frames) + 1]] <- draw(
    if (i == 2) "Step 3: move" else "Step 3 again: move",
    "each X moves to the middle of its color",
    a = steps[[i - 1]]$a, C = steps[[i]]$C, C_old = steps[[i - 1]]$C)
  sw <- steps[[i]]$switched
  frames[[length(frames) + 1]] <- if (sw > 0) {
    draw("Step 2 again: assign", sprintf("%d customers switch color", sw),
         a = steps[[i]]$a, C = steps[[i]]$C, links = TRUE)
  } else {
    draw("Done: nobody switches", "k-means stops; same clusters as two slides ago",
         a = steps[[i]]$a, C = steps[[i]]$C)
  }
}

dir.create("../images/kmeans-steps", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
for (i in seq_along(frames)) {
  ggsave(sprintf("../images/kmeans-steps/step-%02d.png", i), frames[[i]],
         width = 6.4, height = 6, dpi = 150, bg = "white")
}
cat(":::: {.r-stack}\n")
for (i in seq_along(frames)) {
  cat(sprintf("![](images/kmeans-steps/step-%02d.png){%swidth=\"88%%\"}\n\n",
              i, if (i > 1) ".fragment " else ""))
}
cat("::::\n")
```

:::
::: {.column style="width: 39%; margin-left: 5%;"}
1. **Drop** 3 centers at random
2. **Assign**: each customer takes the color of its nearest X
3. **Move** each X to the middle of its color
4. **Repeat** 2 and 3 until nobody switches

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Each click runs one step. Before you click, guess: which customers will
switch color?
:::
:::
:::::

# Segmenting Office-Store Shoppers {.divider}

## A segmentation, step by step {.smaller-80}

Where to start, what to do, and why:

| Step | What to do | Why |
|----|--------|----------|
| **1. Choose the columns** | the six importance ratings | they say what customers **want**, which the store can act on |
| **2. Check the units** | standardize if the columns use different scales | k-means measures distance, so big numbers would dominate |
| **3. Choose k** | run k-means for k = 2 to 10, look for the elbow | more clusters always fit better; the elbow shows when extra clusters stop paying off |
| **4. Run k-means** | k = 3, from many random starts | puts shoppers with similar ratings together |
| **5. Profile** | the average rating of each cluster | k-means only says 1, 2, 3; the averages say what each group wants |
| **6. Name** | a short name for each cluster | managers act on "bargain hunters", not on "cluster 1" |
| **7. Describe** | age, income, and job of each cluster | who they are, and how to reach them |

## Step 1 of 7: the data, and which columns {.smaller-90}

**40 respondents** rated how important six store attributes are to them when
buying office equipment, each on a **1–10** scale:

variety of choice, electronics, furniture, quality of service, low prices,
and return policy

- We also know three things about each respondent: **professional** (0/1),
  **income** (in \$1,000s), and **age**
- We cluster on the **six ratings only**: they say what customers **want**,
  and that is what the store can change (assortment, prices, service)
- The descriptors say **who** customers are. We keep them out so that income
  or age cannot decide the groups: we want "price vs. service", not "young
  vs. old". They come back afterwards, to describe each group

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Data from *R for Marketing Students*.
:::

## Step 2 of 7: check the units {.smaller-90}

Suppose you cluster on **income** (\$15,000 to \$70,000) and **age** (20 to
60):

- Two customers \$1,000 apart in income are 1,000 "units" apart; 25 years
  apart in age, only 25. The distance, and so the clusters, would be
  **all income and no age**
- The fix: **standardize** first, replacing each column with z-scores
  (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation). Then every column
  counts equally

::: {.box-warn}
Standardize whenever the columns have different units. Today's survey
ratings all share the same 1–10 scale, so we can skip it, and keep the
cluster averages in interpretable 1–10 units.
:::

## Step 3 of 7: choose k, the elbow curve

```{r elbow-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_elbow <- ggplot(elbow, aes(x = k, y = wss)) +
  geom_line(color = "#990000", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
  labs(title = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares vs. k",
       x = "Number of clusters k", y = "Total within-cluster SS") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p_elbow
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
For each k, run k-means and add up the squared distances from every point to
its cluster center: the "spread left inside the clusters". Where does the
curve bend?
:::

## Step 3 of 7: reading the elbow {.smaller-90}

```{r elbow-plot-2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.8
p_elbow + labs(title = NULL)
```

- Going from 2 to 3 clusters cuts the within-cluster spread from **636 to
  288**. From 3 to 4 saves only 36 more, and the curve flattens: the
  **elbow is at k = 3**
- More clusters always fit better, so "best fit" cannot pick k: with one
  cluster per customer the fit is perfect and you have learned nothing
- The elbow is a guide, not a law: k must also make **business sense**
  (three campaigns, not nine)

## Steps 4 and 5 of 7: run k-means, profile the clusters {.smaller-90}

We ran k-means on the six ratings with **k = 3**, the elbow's choice. It
split the 40 respondents into clusters of **`r km$size[1]`**, **`r km$size[2]`**,
and **`r km$size[3]`**.
The labels are just 1, 2, 3, in no particular order. The table shows each
cluster's **average rating** of each attribute (1 to 10):

```{r profiles-table}
prof <- dd[, c(list(n = .N), lapply(.SD, function(x) round(mean(x), 1))),
           by = cluster, .SDcols = names(ratings)][order(cluster)]
setnames(prof, c("Cluster", "Respondents", "Variety", "Electronics",
                 "Furniture", "Service", "Low prices", "Return policy"))
knitr::kable(prof, align = "c")
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Read it row by row: what does each cluster rate **high**, and what does it
rate **low**? Try to give each row a name before the next slide.
:::

## Step 6 of 7: name the segments {.smaller-90}

We name each cluster by reading **its row in the profile table** (last
slide): which attributes it rates **high**, and which it rates **low**.

| Cluster (n) | Rates high | Rates low | Our name, and why |
|----|------|------|--------|
| 1 (n = 14) | low prices **8.3**, return policy **6.3** | furniture 1.4, electronics 2.8 | **bargain hunters**: the lowest price, and an easy return if it goes wrong |
| 2 (n = 18) | variety **9.1**, electronics **6.1**, furniture **5.8** | service 2.4, low prices 3.7 | **one-stop shoppers**: a huge range, so they can buy everything (electronics and furniture too) in one store |
| 3 (n = 8) | quality of service **8.5** | low prices 2.5, furniture 1.8 | **service seekers**: good service matters most, price least |

- K-means only says 1, 2, 3. **We** choose the names, by reading the
  averages
- Check the low ratings too: one-stop shoppers care little about price
  (3.7), and service seekers care about it least of all (2.5)

::: {.box}
Every name must be backed by the averages. If a colleague cannot find your
name in the profile table, rename it.
:::

## Step 7 of 7: who is in each segment? {.smaller-90}

The three columns we kept **out** of the clustering describe who landed in
each segment:

| Segment | Professional | Income | Age |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bargain hunters (14) | 50% | \$32,000 | 31 |
| One-stop shoppers (18) | 33% | \$48,000 | 44 |
| Service seekers (8) | **75%** | \$48,000 | **49** |

- Bargain hunters are the **young, lower-income** group; service seekers are
  **older professionals**; one-stop shoppers sit in between with the largest
  headcount
- This is the actionable half: ratings say **what to offer** each segment,
  descriptors say **who and where they are**

::: {.box}
Because these columns played no part in forming the clusters, the
differences across segments are a finding, not something we built in.
:::

# Six Dimensions on One Screen: PCA {.divider}

## Why PCA? {.smaller-90}

We already have the clusters and their averages. Why do anything else?

- **We cannot see six ratings.** With two columns (the 60 customers) our
  eyes could check what k-means did. With six ratings we cannot draw the
  shoppers, so we cannot check whether the clusters really stand apart
- **Many ratings say the same thing.** Shoppers who care about variety
  also care about electronics and furniture (furniture and electronics
  move together: correlation `r round(cor(dd$furniture, dd$electronics), 2)`).
  Three columns, one idea: **assortment**. PCA finds the few big ideas
  behind many ratings
- **Managers think in maps.** A two-axis map shows who is close to whom,
  customers or brands, and where the **gaps** are

::: {.box}
PCA turns six ratings into a two-axis **map** that keeps most of the
information. We use it to **see** the segments, and to find the few
dimensions customers really differ on.
:::

## PCA: six ratings, one map {.smaller-90}

- PCA replaces the six ratings with **new axes**, called **PC1, PC2**, and
  so on. Each new axis is a **mix** of the six ratings, the way a GPA is a
  mix of grades
- The axes come **in order**: PC1 captures the biggest differences between
  shoppers, PC2 the next biggest, and so on
- Keep the first two, and every shopper gets a spot on a **map**

::: {.box}
You do not need to know how the computer finds the axes. You need to answer
two questions: **how many axes to keep**, and **what each axis means**.
:::

## How many axes to keep? {.smaller-90}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 48%;"}
```{r pc-shares}
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
shares <- data.table(pc = paste0("PC", 1:6),
                     share = round(100 * summary(pca)$importance[2, ]))
ggplot(shares, aes(x = pc, y = share, fill = pc %in% c("PC1", "PC2"))) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(share, "%")), vjust = -0.4, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#990000", `FALSE` = "grey70"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60), breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Share of the differences each axis keeps", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::
::: {.column style="width: 47%; margin-left: 5%;"}
- Each bar says how much of the differences between shoppers one axis
  keeps. The six bars add up to 100% (give or take rounding)
- **PC1** keeps **`r shares$share[1]`%** and **PC2** **`r shares$share[2]`%**:
  together **`r shares$share[1] + shares$share[2]`%**. After PC2 the bars
  drop to `r shares$share[3]`% and below
- The rule: keep axes until the bars get **small** (an elbow, like
  the one in segmentation step 3), and check that the ones you keep add up to **most** of the total
:::
:::::

::: {.box}
Two axes keep `r shares$share[1] + shares$share[2]`% here, so the map tells
most of the story. If they kept, say, 40%, the map would hide more than it
shows.
:::

## What do the two axes mean? {.smaller-90}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r loadings-plot}
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.8
arrow_scale <- 3
ggplot(loadings, aes(x = PC1 * arrow_scale, y = PC2 * arrow_scale, label = attribute)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1 * arrow_scale, yend = PC2 * arrow_scale),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), color = "#990000") +
  geom_text_repel(size = 4.5, seed = 1) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "The six ratings as arrows", x = "PC1", y = "PC2") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Each arrow is one rating. It points to where shoppers who rate it **high**
end up on the map:

- **PC1** (left vs. right): **three** arrows point left: variety,
  electronics, and furniture. Name the axis by what the three share: left
  means "wants a **big assortment**". "Furniture" alone would leave out the
  other two
- **PC2** (up vs. down): **low prices** reaches highest, **quality of
  service** reaches lowest. Up means "cares about price, not service";
  down, the reverse
:::
:::::

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
PCA could just as well have flipped left and right, or up and down. What
matters is which arrows point the same way, and which point opposite ways.
:::

## The map: 40 shoppers, colored by cluster {.smaller-90}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r cluster-map}
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_map <- ggplot(scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(values = seg_cols, labels = seg_labs, name = NULL) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = range(c(scores$PC1, loadings$PC1 * 3)) + c(-0.4, 0.4),
              ylim = range(c(scores$PC2, loadings$PC2 * 3)) + c(-0.4, 0.4)) +
  labs(title = "Shoppers on the PCA Map", x = "PC1", y = "PC2") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
p_map
```
:::
::: {.column style="width: 40%; margin-left: 5%;"}
Each dot is a shopper, placed by PCA. The colors are the k-means clusters.

PCA drew the map; k-means picked the colors. The two never talked to each
other.

::: {.muted}
Do the colors form regions?
:::
:::
:::::

## The map: reading it {.smaller-90}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 55%;"}
```{r biplot}
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
arrow_scale <- 3
p_map +
  geom_segment(data = loadings,
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1 * arrow_scale, yend = PC2 * arrow_scale),
               inherit.aes = FALSE,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), color = "grey40") +
  geom_text_repel(data = loadings,
                  aes(x = PC1 * arrow_scale, y = PC2 * arrow_scale, label = attribute),
                  inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.8, color = "grey30", seed = 1)
```
:::
::: {.column style="width: 40%; margin-left: 5%;"}
- The clusters sit in **separate regions**, each at the tip of the arrows
  its profile predicted: bargain hunters by *low prices*, one-stop shoppers
  by *variety and furniture*, service seekers by *quality of service*
- Why this matters: k-means **always** returns groups (ask for 3, you get
  3), even when there are none. PCA never saw the clusters. If the colors
  still form separate clouds on its map, the groups are **real**. If they
  were mixed together, k-means would just have cut one blob into pieces
:::
:::::

## A second dataset: four brands {.smaller-90}

A **separate survey**. Respondents rated four
office-equipment **brands** on six things. Each number is the **average**
rating:

```{r brand-data}
bd <- copy(brands)
setnames(bd, c("Brand", "Large choice", "Low prices", "Service quality",
               "Product quality", "Convenience", "Preference"))
knitr::kable(bd, align = "lcccccc")
```

- **Rows are brands** now, not shoppers. Same problem as before: six
  columns, and a screen has two axes
- **Preference** is how much respondents like the brand overall
- Same PCA, read the same way: which brands sit close together, and which
  arrows point at each brand?

## Four brands on one map: a perceptual map

```{r brand-map}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
arrow_scale_b <- 2
# attribute labels sit just past their own arrow tip, pointing outward
att <- loadings_b[, .(x = PC1 * arrow_scale_b, y = PC2 * arrow_scale_b, label = attribute)]
att[, ang := atan2(y, x)]
att[, `:=`(lx = x + 0.12 * cos(ang), ly = y + 0.12 * sin(ang),
           hj = (1 - cos(ang)) / 2, vj = (1 - sin(ang)) / 2)]
# brand labels placed by hand: above or below each point, clear of the arrows
bl <- scores_b[, .(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = brand)]
bl[, side := fifelse(label %in% c("PaperNCo", "OfficeEquipment"), -1, 1)]
bl[, `:=`(ly = y + 0.24 * side, vj = fifelse(side > 0, 0, 1),
          hj = fifelse(label == "OfficeStar", 0.85, fifelse(label == "Supermarket", 0.2, 0.5)))]
p_brand <- ggplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 3, color = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(data = att, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), color = "grey45") +
  geom_text(data = att, aes(x = lx, y = ly, label = label, hjust = hj, vjust = vj),
            size = 4, color = "grey25") +
  geom_point(data = scores_b, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2), color = "#990000", size = 4) +
  geom_text(data = bl, aes(x = x, y = ly, label = label, hjust = hj, vjust = vj),
            color = "#990000", fontface = "bold", size = 5.2) +
  coord_fixed(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Perceptual Map: Four Office-Equipment Brands", x = "PC1", y = "PC2") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p_brand
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
Each red dot is a **brand**; each arrow is one of the six ratings. Which
brands compete head-to-head? Who owns which attribute?
:::

## The perceptual map: reading it {.smaller-90}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 52%;"}
```{r brand-map-2}
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
p_brand + labs(title = NULL)
```
:::
::: {.column style="width: 43%; margin-left: 5%;"}
- **OfficeStar** sits alone on the right, next to *service quality,
  product quality, large choice*, and **preference**: the strong brand
  people like best
- **Supermarket** is its mirror image, on the left by *low prices* and
  *convenience*. **PaperNCo** owns the cheap corner; **OfficeEquipment**
  leans on convenience, with no clear strength
- Two axes keep **98%** of the differences between the brands: the map is
  almost the whole story
:::
:::::

::: {.box}
Perceptual maps answer positioning questions: who are my real competitors
(neighbors on the map), what do I own (my nearest arrows), and where is the
**gap** nobody occupies.
:::

## Clustering and PCA, side by side {.smaller-90}

| | K-means | PCA |
|---|---|---|
| Question | which customers belong together? | how do I show six ratings on one map? |
| Output | a **group label** per customer (1, 2, 3) | **two scores** (PC1, PC2) per customer |
| You choose | the columns, and k | the columns, and how many axes to keep |
| You read it with | the averages (profile table) | the arrows |
| Marketing use | segmentation | perceptual maps; seeing the segments |

::: {.box-warn}
Three cautions for both methods:

- **Standardize** when the columns use different units
- Clusters and axes mean **nothing** until you read them: the averages for
  clusters, the arrows for axes
- Clusters **describe** customers; they do not explain them. Service
  seekers are older on average, but that does not mean age makes people
  want service. It only tells us who tends to be in the group
:::

## From clustering to PCA: the steps, and why {.smaller-80}

| Step | What to do | Why |
|----|---------|----------|
| **1. Pick the columns** | what customers want (the ratings); standardize if the scales differ | groups built on needs, with fair distances |
| **2. Find the groups** | choose k with the elbow, then run k-means | shoppers with similar ratings end up together |
| **3. Read the means** | the average rating of each cluster, then name each one | what each group wants, in exact numbers |
| **4. Describe** | age, income, and job of each cluster | who they are, and how to reach them |
| **5. Check the axes** | run PCA; keep two axes if they hold most of the differences | a map is only useful if it tells most of the story |
| **6. Map and compare** | plot the shoppers on PC1 and PC2, color them by cluster, add the arrows | see whether the groups really separate, and what separates them |

::: {.box}
Steps 3 and 6 **check each other**. The means give exact numbers, one
attribute at a time; the map shows all the shoppers at once. The check: each
cluster should sit next to the arrows of what it rates **highest**. Here it
does (bargain hunters, who rate low prices 8.3, sit by the low-prices
arrow), so the segments are real, not something k-means made up.
:::
